meaning.evidence: All points kept across the four scam types and their protections: "Demand ya pay up on the spot with gift cards, crypto, or wire transfers", "Always check the website URL ends in .gov."

sense.evidence: "dodgy", "fair dinkum", "suss", "Sting ya fees" all carry the right sense; "Hurry ya up to click a link" fits urge.

authenticity.evidence: Natural enough, with dropped g's throughout ("cookin'", "handin'"), but "Sting ya fees" drops the "for" Aussies would use, and "Hurry ya up to click" is slightly off.

register.evidence: Strong but not full level 5: lots of drawl and "fair dinkum", "suss", "ring up", yet several bullets stay plain ("Ask for personal details like Social Security numbers or bank details"). No swearing (vulgarity 2 permits, does not require).

tone.evidence: Keeps it a serious consumer warning under the slang.

flow.evidence: Reads easily; minor clunk in "Sting ya fees for services".

variety.evidence: Leans on "makin' out" ("Make out there's an urgent problem", "the scammer's makin' out to be", "makin' out they're government officials") and "dodgy" ("dodgy payments", "dodgy messages", "dodgy websites").

essence.evidence: Clearly the scam-awareness page, structure intact.

problems.quote: Sting ya fees for services that are free on the official sites
problems.original: Charge fees for services that are free on official sites
problems.why: Sting someone for fees is the idiom; dropping for reads off.

problems.quote: Report dodgy messages to the agency the scammer's makin' out to be
problems.original: Report fraudulent messages to the agency the scammer is trying to represent
problems.why: Makin' out and dodgy repeated across the text.

A.summary: Solid and safe, a notch under the brief, with some repeated terms.

meaning.evidence: All points kept: "Want the dosh right this second, by gift cards, cryptocurrency, or wire transfers", "Dob in suss profiles on social media to the social media platform."

sense.evidence: Mostly exact ("swifties", "shonks", "dob in", "cough up"), but "Keepin' yer wits about ya on their tricks" strains for staying informed, and "Reckon there's some urgent drama" fits claim loosely.

authenticity.evidence: Rich, mostly genuine idiom ("don't know from a bar of soap", "pull a swifty" as "swifties they pull"), though "slanter websites" is obscure and dated, and the density edges toward showy.

register.evidence: Full level 5 weight: "Shonks might give ya a ring", "Want the dosh right this second", "knocked together". No swearing (permitted, not required).

tone.evidence: Still a warning, though "some urgent drama" lightens the threat a little.

flow.evidence: Mostly flows; "Keepin' yer wits about ya on their tricks is yer best defence" is a clumsy join.

variety.evidence: Wide range: "swifties", "shonks", "slanter", "dosh", "cough up", "dob in"; only "dob in" repeats.

problems.quote: Keepin' yer wits about ya on their tricks is yer best defence.
problems.original: Staying informed about these tactics is your best defense.
problems.why: Keeping your wits about you means staying alert, not keeping informed; the join with on their tricks is awkward.

problems.quote: Some scams use slanter websites knocked together
problems.original: Some scams use fraudulent websites designed to look like official government pages
problems.why: Slanter is obscure and dated; many Australians would not know it.

problems.quote: Reckon there's some urgent drama with yer benefits or tax return
problems.original: Claim there is an urgent issue with your benefits or tax return
problems.why: Drama makes the scam threat sound trivial.

B.summary: The fullest, most varied yarn; a few strained or obscure picks.

meaning.evidence: Everything kept; "Nine times outta ten they'll" slightly firms up "often" but remains colour.

sense.evidence: "rorts", "the real deal", "fair dinkum", "suss", "Want payin' on the spot" all fit.

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like a real Australian talking: "So here's a rundown of the most common rorts goin' round", "Report suss profiles on social media to the platform they're on."

register.evidence: Heavy drawl and idiom, close to level 5, though some bullets stay plain ("Always check the website URL ends in .gov."). No swearing (permitted).

flow.evidence: Smooth: "Hang up, then ring the official number listed on the Login.gov or agency website."

variety.evidence: Varied, with "dodgy" three times ("a dodgy payment", "Report dodgy messages", "run dodgy websites").

problems.quote: Some scams run dodgy websites made up to look just like official government pages.
problems.original: Some scams use fraudulent websites designed to look like official government pages.

C.summary: Natural, smooth and faithful; just short of full level 5.
